learningOutcomes: Distinguish path length, displacement, speed and velocity.
Interpret x–t and v–t graphs (slope and area).
Apply kinematic equations for constant acceleration.
Solve free-fall / vertical throw problems with sign convention.
Use stopping distance and reaction-time ideas in numericals.

cheatSheet.oneLiner: Rectilinear motion: velocity from dx/dt, acceleration from dv/dt; for constant a use the three kinematic equations with careful signs.
mustKnowBullets: Motion along a straight line is rectilinear motion; treat bodies as point objects when size ≪ distance moved.
Instantaneous velocity v = dx/dt = slope of x–t graph; speed = |v|.
Instantaneous acceleration a = dv/dt = slope of v–t graph.
Area under v–t curve = displacement in that interval.
For constant a: v = v0 + at; x = v0 t + (1/2)at²; v² = v0² + 2ax (if x0 = 0).
If start at x0: replace x by (x − x0).
Free fall near Earth: a = −g if upward is positive (g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻²).
Zero velocity at an instant does NOT imply zero acceleration (e.g. top of throw).
Kinematic equations hold only for constant acceleration; definitions of v and a always hold.

highlights.text: Motion is change in position of an object with time.
In Kinematics, we study ways to describe motion without going into the causes of motion.
highlights.whyItMatters: Separates Ch 2–3 from Laws of Motion (Ch 4).

highlights.text: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as Δt → 0; v = dx/dt.
Instantaneous speed at an instant equals the magnitude of instantaneous velocity at that instant.
highlights.whyItMatters: Speed vs velocity trap in assertion-reason.

highlights.text: Average acceleration is change in velocity divided by the time interval; a_avg = Δv/Δt.
The area under the velocity–time curve equals the displacement over that time interval.
For uniformly accelerated rectilinear motion: v = v0 + at; x = v0 t + ½ at²; v² = v0² + 2ax.
highlights.whyItMatters: The three equations every student must automate.

highlights.text: The sign of acceleration does not by itself tell whether speed is increasing or decreasing — compare directions of v and a.
Zero velocity at an instant does not imply zero acceleration (particle at top of trajectory).
Kinematic equations are true only when magnitude and direction of acceleration are constant.
highlights.whyItMatters: Stops misuse of SUVAT for variable a.

highlights.text: Average speed over an interval is ≥ magnitude of average velocity over the same interval.
Stopping distance ds = v0² / (2a) for deceleration a (with v = 0).
Relative velocity of object A with respect to object B, both moving along the same straight line, is v_AB = v_A − v_B (a vector subtraction; in 1D, a simple algebraic subtraction with sign).
highlights.whyItMatters: A distinct NCERT section (2.5) entirely separate from the kinematic equations — tested via 'two trains/cars approach or recede' style problems.

highlights.text: If two objects move in the SAME direction, their relative velocity is the difference of their speeds; if they move in OPPOSITE directions, their relative velocity is the SUM of their speeds (using consistent sign convention, this falls out automatically from v_A − v_B).
highlights.whyItMatters: Common shortcut students misapply — always safer to assign a sign convention and subtract algebraically than to memorise 'add for opposite, subtract for same'.

definitions.definition: Motion of an object along a straight line.
Change in position vector; for 1D, x2 − x1 with sign.
Total length of the path actually travelled (always ≥ 0).
Limit of Δx/Δt as Δt → 0; equal to dx/dt.
Rate of change of velocity with time; a = dv/dt.
Acceleration constant in magnitude and direction.
Motion under gravity alone (air resistance neglected); a = −g if up is positive.
The velocity of one object as observed from a reference frame attached to another object; for motion along a line, v_AB = v_A − v_B.

formulas.name: Instantaneous velocity
formulas.plain: velocity = rate of change of position
formulas.whenToUse: When position is given as a function of time, or as slope of x–t graph.
commonMistakes: Confusing average velocity with instantaneous velocity

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: x given as polynomial in t → find v at an instant.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: x = 2t³ − 3t; find v at t = 1 s.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Graph given; velocity = slope of tangent at that instant.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Read rise/run of the tangent at the required time.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: From an x–t curve, estimate v at t = 4 s.

formulas.audioScript: Instantaneous velocity is how fast position is changing right now. On a position–time graph, that is the slope of the tangent. If you have a formula for x of t, differentiate it.

formulas.name: Average velocity and speed
formulas.plain: average velocity uses displacement; average speed uses path length
formulas.whenToUse: Go-and-return trips, drunkard walk, market problems.
commonMistakes: Using path length in average velocity
Saying average speed is zero on a round trip

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Net displacement may be zero while path length is not.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: v_avg = 0 if back to start; speed_avg = total path / time.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Walk 2.5 km to market and back; find average velocity and average speed for full trip.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Need displacement and path for a sub-interval of the journey.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Compute x(t) positions at interval ends; sum path segments.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Man walks to market at 5 km/h and returns at 7.5 km/h; find averages for 0–40 min.

formulas.audioScript: Average velocity cares only about where you started and ended. Average speed cares about every metre you walked. On a round trip, average velocity can be zero while average speed is not.

formulas.name: Instantaneous acceleration
formulas.plain: acceleration = rate of change of velocity
formulas.whenToUse: Slope of v–t graph; differentiating v(t).
commonMistakes: Mixing sign of a with 'speeding up'

questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: a = Δv/Δt from the straight v–t line.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: v increases from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s uniformly; find a.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: At highest point of a throw, v = 0 but a = −g.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Acceleration is slope of v–t, still −g.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A ball thrown up: acceleration at the topmost point?

formulas.audioScript: Acceleration tells how velocity is changing. On a velocity–time graph it is the slope. A particle can be momentarily at rest and still accelerating — think of a ball at the top of its path.

formulas.name: Displacement from v–t area
formulas.plain: displacement equals area under velocity–time graph
formulas.whenToUse: Any v–t graph question asking distance/displacement.
commonMistakes: Treating area below t-axis as positive path without care

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Constant v or uniformly changing v → simple geometry.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Area = base × height or ½ base × height.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: v = 10 m/s for 5 s; find displacement.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Motion reverses; net displacement is algebraic sum of areas.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Areas below axis are negative displacement.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: v–t graph goes positive then negative; find net displacement.

formulas.audioScript: The area between the velocity–time curve and the time axis is displacement. Above the axis means positive displacement; below means negative. For distance travelled, add absolute areas.

formulas.name: Kinematic set (constant a)
formulas.latex: v = v_0 + at,\quad x = v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2,\quad v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ax
formulas.plain: three equations linking v0, v, a, t, x for constant acceleration
formulas.whenToUse: Uniform acceleration along a straight line — braking, free fall, inclined with const a.
commonMistakes: Using equations when a is not constant
Wrong sign for a or v0

questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Pick the equation missing the unknown you do not have.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Car brakes from 20 m/s with a = −4 m/s²; find stopping distance.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Choose +up; a = −g; split or use one quadratic in t.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Same three equations with signed quantities.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Ball thrown up at 20 m/s from 25 m height; time to hit ground?

formulas.audioScript: For constant acceleration you get three friends: v equals v zero plus a t; x equals v zero t plus half a t squared; and v squared equals v zero squared plus two a x. Choose the equation that avoids the quantity you do not know. Always fix your positive direction first.

formulas.name: Free fall
formulas.plain: released from rest: downward if up is positive uses minus g
formulas.whenToUse: Objects dropped or thrown near Earth, air neglected.
commonMistakes: Taking g positive downward while also taking up as positive inconsistently

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: v0 = 0, find t or speed on hitting ground.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Drop a ball from 45 m; find time to ground (g = 10).

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Ruler falls distance d before catch; find tr.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Ruler falls 21 cm before you catch it; estimate reaction time.

formulas.audioScript: In free fall we ignore air resistance. If upward is positive, acceleration is minus g. From rest, speed grows as g t and distance fallen is half g t squared.

formulas.name: Stopping distance
formulas.latex: d_s = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2a}\quad (v=0,\ a>0 \text{ as magnitude of deceleration})
formulas.plain: stopping distance proportional to square of initial speed
formulas.whenToUse: Vehicles braking to rest; speed-limit reasoning.
commonMistakes: Thinking doubling speed doubles stopping distance (it quadruples)

questionPatterns.exampleStem: Bike at 72 km/h brakes at 5 m/s²; find stopping distance.
If speed doubles at same deceleration, how does stopping distance change?

formulas.audioScript: When brakes bring you to rest, stopping distance is v zero squared over two a. Double the speed and stopping distance becomes four times larger — that is why speed limits matter.

formulas.name: Average velocity (const a)
formulas.plain: for constant acceleration, average velocity is arithmetic mean of initial and final velocities
formulas.whenToUse: Shortcut: x = v_avg × t when a is constant.
commonMistakes: Using (v0+v)/2 when acceleration is not constant

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Know v0, v, t under const a.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Speed rises uniformly from 10 to 30 m/s in 4 s; find displacement.

questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Must integrate or use area under actual v–t curve.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Why is (u+v)/2 invalid for arbitrary v–t shapes?

formulas.audioScript: Only when acceleration is constant is average velocity the simple average of initial and final velocities. Otherwise use displacement over time from the actual motion.

formulas.name: Relative velocity
formulas.plain: relative velocity of A with respect to B = velocity of A minus velocity of B

symbols.meaning: velocities of A and B in a common (ground) frame, with sign

formulas.whenToUse: Two objects moving along the same line — trains, cars, or a bullet fired from a moving vehicle — asking how fast one appears to move relative to the other.
commonMistakes: Forgetting sign convention: opposite-direction velocities effectively ADD once you subtract a negative number; same-direction velocities partially cancel.
Confusing v_AB (A relative to B) with v_BA (B relative to A) — they are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Assign a positive direction, write each velocity with its correct sign, then subtract.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A police van moving at 30 km/h fires a bullet (muzzle speed 150 m/s) at a thief's car speeding away at 192 km/h in the same direction. Find the velocity with which the bullet hits the car.

formulas.audioScript: Relative velocity is just a subtraction — but the sign convention does all the real work, so always fix a positive direction first and write every velocity, including the 'reference' object's, with its correct sign before subtracting.

stages.question: What is instantaneous velocity?
stages.answer: Rate of change of position with time; slope of x–t tangent.

flashcards.audioScript: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero. On a graph, read the slope of the tangent.

stages.question: Is instantaneous speed always equal to |instantaneous velocity|?
solutionSteps: Over an interval, average speed ≥ |average velocity|
stages.answer: Yes at an instant; averages over an interval may differ.

flashcards.audioScript: At a single instant, speed is just the size of velocity. Over a longer trip, average speed can be larger than the magnitude of average velocity.
Acceleration is change in velocity per second, so metres per second squared.

stages.question: What does the area under a v–t graph represent?
stages.interpretation: NCERT geometric meaning of the graph.
solutionSteps: For constant v, area = vT = displacement

flashcards.audioScript: Area under the velocity–time curve is displacement. Watch signs if the curve dips below the time axis.

stages.question: Car goes from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s with constant a. Find a and distance.
stages.interpretation: Const a from rest → use v = at and x = ½at².

flashcards.audioScript: From rest, acceleration is final speed over time: 4 metres per second squared. Distance is half a t squared: 50 metres.

stages.question: Why does doubling speed (same brakes) multiply stopping distance by 4?
solutionSteps: From v² = v0² − 2a ds with v=0
stages.answer: Because stopping distance depends on the square of initial speed.

flashcards.audioScript: Stopping distance goes as speed squared. Twice the speed needs four times the distance to stop at the same deceleration.

stages.question: Ball thrown upward: acceleration at the highest point?
stages.interpretation: v = 0 there but gravity still acts.

flashcards.audioScript: At the top the ball is briefly at rest, but gravity has not switched off. Acceleration remains g downward.

stages.question: A particle has negative acceleration. Is it necessarily slowing down?
stages.interpretation: Compare directions of v and a.
solutionSteps: If v and a same sign → speeding up
Sign of a alone is not enough
stages.answer: No — it depends on the sign of velocity relative to a.

flashcards.audioScript: Negative acceleration only means acceleration points toward the negative axis. If velocity is also negative, the particle is speeding up.

stages.question: Ball thrown up at 20 m/s from a 25 m tower (g=10). Time to hit ground?
stages.interpretation: One quadratic with y=0, y0=25, v0=20, a=−10.
stages.formula: y = y_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2

flashcards.audioScript: Place origin at ground, up positive. Then zero equals 25 plus 20 t minus 5 t squared. The positive root is 5 seconds.

stages.question: Path length versus displacement for a round trip back to start?
stages.answer: Displacement 0; path length equals total distance walked.

flashcards.audioScript: Coming back home, your displacement is zero but you still walked a long path length.

stages.question: Ruler falls d = 21 cm before catch. Estimate reaction time (g=9.8).
stages.interpretation: Free fall from rest: d = ½gt².

flashcards.audioScript: The ruler falls freely. Distance is half g t squared, so reaction time is square root of two d over g — roughly point two one seconds for 21 centimetres.

stages.question: For uniform acceleration, shape of x–t and v–t graphs?
solutionSteps: a const ⇒ v–t is straight line
x is quadratic in t ⇒ parabola on x–t

flashcards.audioScript: Constant acceleration makes velocity change linearly with time — a straight v–t graph — while position follows a parabola on the x–t graph.

conceptWarmup: Can average speed be less than |average velocity|?

basic.question: A particle’s position is x = 5 + 2t (x in m, t in s). Find velocity at t = 3 s.
basic.audioScript: Differentiate x with respect to t. The slope is 2, so velocity is constantly 2 metres per second.

basic.question: Average speed if you walk 100 m east in 50 s and 100 m west in 50 s?
basic.audioScript: You walked two hundred metres in one hundred seconds, so average speed is 2 metres per second. Net displacement is zero, so average velocity is zero.

basic.question: Speed rises uniformly from 0 to 30 m/s in 6 s. Find acceleration.
basic.audioScript: Change in velocity over time is 30 divided by 6, so acceleration is 5 metres per second squared.

basic.question: Using v = v0 + at: v0 = 10 m/s, a = 2 m/s², t = 4 s. Find v.
basic.audioScript: Final velocity is initial plus a t: 10 plus 8 equals 18 metres per second.

intermediate.question: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with a = −5 m/s². Find stopping distance.
intermediate.audioScript: Set final speed zero. Four hundred equals 10 x, so stopping distance is 40 metres.

intermediate.question: Object dropped from rest from 80 m (g=10). Find time to hit ground and impact speed.
intermediate.interpretation: Free fall; up positive or down positive consistently.
steps: Take down positive: y = ½gt² → 80 = 5t² → t = 4 s
intermediate.audioScript: From rest, distance is half g t squared. With g = 10, t is 4 seconds and impact speed is 40 metres per second.

intermediate.question: v–t graph: 0 to 10 m/s linearly in 2 s, then constant 10 m/s for 3 s. Find displacement.
intermediate.audioScript: Add the triangular area of 10 metres to the rectangular area of 30 metres to get 40 metres displacement.

intermediate.question: Reaction time: ruler falls 20 cm. Take g = 10 m/s². Find tr.
intermediate.audioScript: Twenty centimetres is 0.2 metres. Half of 10 times t squared equals 0.2, so t is 0.2 seconds.

advanced.question: Ball thrown upward at 20 m/s from a 25 m high building. Take g = 10. Find (a) max rise above launch and (b) time to hit ground.
advanced.interpretation: NCERT Example 2.3 style; signs with up positive.
advanced.audioScript: At the top, speed is zero so height above launch is 20 metres. From ground as origin, solve the quadratic; time to hit ground is 5 seconds.

advanced.question: Show distances fallen in successive equal times from rest are in ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : …
advanced.audioScript: From rest, position grows as time squared. The extra distance in each equal tick is the next odd number — Galileo’s law.

advanced.question: x = 0.08 t³ (t in s, x in m). Estimate v at t = 4 s using Δt → 0 idea (or exact derivative).
advanced.audioScript: Differentiate 0.08 t cubed to get 0.24 t squared. At 4 seconds that is 3.84 metres per second — the limiting slope of the position graph.

advanced.question: A drunkard takes 5 steps forward and 3 back, each step 1 m and 1 s. How long to fall in a pit 13 m away?
advanced.interpretation: Net +2 m every 8 s; then final approach.
steps: Each cycle of 8 steps: net +2 m in 8 s
Need 3 m more: 3 forward steps (cannot use full cycle)
advanced.audioScript: Every eight seconds he gains only two metres. After forty seconds he is ten metres along; three more forward steps take him into the pit at 43 seconds.

problemLadder.transferPrompt: Invent one new NEET-style MCQ that needs both a v–t area argument and a kinematic equation with constant a.

studentTutorPrompt:
You are my Physics tutor for NEET, JEE and KCET for NCERT Class 11 Chapter 2: Motion in a Straight Line only.

Session flow:
1) Ask my goal: revise concepts / formula drill / weak area (graphs, free fall, signs, braking).
2) Quiz definitions first (displacement vs path length, instantaneous v and a, area under v–t) — no heavy calculation.
3) Basic numericals: one formula at a time (v=dx/dt, a=dv/dt, SUVAT plug-ins).
4) Intermediate: graph areas, stopping distance, free-fall timing.
5) Advanced: vertical throw with building height, odd-number rule, drunkard/pit, sign-convention traps.
6) After each wrong answer show: Interpretation → Formula link → Steps.
7) Offer flashcard mode (Q → interpretation → formula → steps → answer) and formula-view mode.
8) Stay inside this chapter unless I ask to link to Laws of Motion or 2D motion.

Start by asking my goal and one warm-up: “Does zero velocity mean zero acceleration? Why?”

selfCheck.q: Acceleration at top of a vertical throw?
